🇨🇦 THE BANK OF CANADA IS HOLDING $1.6 BILLION THAT BELONGS TO PEOPLE WHO HAVEN’T CLAIMED IT.

AND MOST CANADIANS HAVE NO IDEA THEY CAN SEARCH FOR THEIR MONEY.

Here’s something I found fascinating.

As of December 31, 2025, the Bank of Canada was holding 3.6 MILLION unclaimed bank balances worth approximately $1.6 BILLION.

Not government grants.

Not taxpayer subsidies.

Money left behind in old bank accounts, deposits and other eligible financial instruments.

Maybe someone opened an account 20 years ago.

Moved to another province.

Changed banks.

Forgot about a deposit.

Or died without telling their family the account existed.

After 10 years of inactivity, federally regulated banks generally transfer eligible unclaimed balances to the Bank of Canada.

Now here’s the interesting part.

Let’s look at the numbers.

🏦 Total unclaimed balances: $1.6 BILLION

👥 Number of balances: 3.6 MILLION

💰 Total claims paid in 2025: $20 MILLION

📋 Number of claims paid: 1,937

That’s an average payment of approximately $10,325 per successful claim.

Of course, individual claims vary enormously.

But here’s another detail.

The Bank of Canada generally holds balances under $1,000 for 30 years.

Balances of $1,000 or more can be held for 100 years.

After that, unclaimed funds are transferred to the federal government.

And the Bank of Canada doesn’t automatically notify owners when their money arrives.

HERE’S SOMETHING YOU CAN ACTUALLY DO TODAY.

Visit the Bank of Canada’s official Unclaimed Properties website.

Search your name.

Search previous names.

Check for deceased family members whose estates you’re legally authorized to manage.

The search is free.

You may find absolutely nothing.

Or you might discover money you didn’t know existed.

We spend our lives trying to earn more money.

Maybe we should occasionally check whether we’ve forgotten some of the money we already earned.

Oseola McCarty was a Mississippi philanthropist who donated most of her life savings, $150,000, to the University of Southern Mississippi to provide scholarships for African American students in need. 

A seamstress and washerwoman who was paid mostly in dollar bills and loose change her entire life, McCarty was praised for her generosity and received many awards, including an honorary degree from the university. McCarty was born on March 7, 1908, in Shubuta, Mississippi. 

McCarty was born on March 7, 1908, in Shubuta, Mississippi. She was raised in nearby Hattiesburg by her aunt and grandmother, both of whom cleaned houses, cooked, and took in washing to make money. McCarty quit school in the sixth grade in order to care for her ailing aunt, and she took over the domestic work that she would do for the rest of her life. McCarty, who never married and had no children, lived frugally in a house without air conditioning. She never had a car or learned to drive, so she walked everywhere, including the grocery store that was one mile from her home. Her thriftiness would become legendary: she cut the toes out of shoes that did not fit right, and she bound her well-worn Bible with Scotch tape.
When she was eight years old, McCarty opened a savings account at a bank in Hattiesburg and began depositing the coins she earned from her laundry work. She would eventually open accounts in several local banks. By the time McCarty retired at age 86, her hands crippled by arthritis, she had saved $280,000. She set aside a pension for herself to live on, a donation to her church, and small inheritances for three of her relatives. The remainder—$150,000—she donated to the University of Southern Mississippi, a school that had remained all-white until the 1960s.
